title: Wind-Down Drills
blurb: Three sequences for taking a live system offline — safely, legally, and only for as long as it needs to stay down.
source: AIGP BOK IV.C · AIGP Study Guide (SG) §Domain IV.C · scored backup in G14 (Live-System Duty Roster) and G16 (The Recall)

ladders.title: Retiring a system
ladders.prompt: Order the steps for responsibly retiring a live AI system.

steps.label: Assess dependencies + fallback options
steps.detail: Before touching anything live, map what depends on the system — upstream data feeds, downstream processes, other teams' workflows — and confirm a fallback exists so retirement doesn't create an outage (SG-C12-Q008).

steps.label: Notify stakeholders + plan controlled deactivation
steps.detail: The first step in a driven retirement is telling the people affected and building a deactivation plan, not simply flipping a switch (SG-AT-Q034).

steps.label: Graduated deactivation with human backup
steps.detail: For critical infrastructure, wind down in stages rather than all at once, with a human-run fallback covering the gap — the same discipline used for critical systems generally.

steps.label: Archive, don't delete, for legal/audit
steps.detail: Preserve the retired system's data, models, and logs rather than deleting them — regulators and auditors may need to reconstruct what the system did and why, long after it stops running (SG-C12-Q007).

steps.label: Record like a black-box investigation, with named decision-makers
steps.detail: Log the exact trigger, who authorized the shutdown, and the retirement rationale in the same evidentiary style as an incident investigation — a single auditable source of truth naming who had the authority to act (SG).

ladders.title: Incident lifecycle
ladders.prompt: Order the response to a live AI incident from first detection to closing the loop.

steps.label: Detect
steps.detail: An alert, a monitoring signal, or a complaint surfaces that something is wrong — this starts the clock on everything that follows.

steps.label: Contain / quarantine first
steps.detail: Before investigating causes or drafting communications, stop the harm from spreading: quarantine the model and notify legal/compliance immediately. Containment beats investigation, recovery, or communication as the very next move — jumping straight to root-cause analysis while the system keeps causing harm is the recorded exam trap.

steps.label: Notify legal/compliance (+72-hour breach clock where personal data)
steps.detail: Where the incident involves personal data, a GDPR controller must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach — incident response and notification procedures must be built to hit that deadline, not treated as a technical afterthought (SG).

steps.label: Root-cause (Five Whys / fault tree)
steps.detail: Use a formal analysis framework — the 'Five Whys' method or fault-tree analysis — to drill down to the underlying cause instead of stopping at the surface-level symptom (SG).

steps.label: CAPA
steps.detail: Record corrective and preventive actions in a central system with assigned owners, deadlines, and verification steps, so the root cause is actually closed out, not just diagnosed.

steps.label: Blameless retrospective + proactive disclosure with lessons learned
steps.detail: Run a cross-functional, blameless review of what happened and why, and proactively disclose technical details and lessons learned rather than waiting to be asked — this is what turns a patched symptom into a documented, defensible improvement.

ladders.title: Restart after the switch
ladders.prompt: Order the steps for safely bringing a deactivated system back online.

steps.label: Verify the fix
steps.detail: Confirm the specific defect that triggered deactivation has actually been corrected before anything else moves forward — resumption depends on fixes being verified, not merely attempted (SG).

steps.label: Re-test with first-release rigor
steps.detail: Put the fixed system through the same full testing it faced before its original launch — performance, robustness, security, fairness — retesting confirms safety and compliance from scratch, it doesn't get a shortcut because the system has run before (SG).

steps.label: Cross-functional approval
steps.detail: The system resumes only once cross-functional teams — not a single engineer or team lead — approve the restart, closing the loop that started with named decision-makers authorizing the shutdown.

steps.label: Staged canary/blue-green re-rollout behind feature flags
steps.detail: Bring the system back gradually — a canary release or blue-green deployment gated by feature flags — so exposure can be dialed back instantly if the problem resurfaces, rather than flipping every user back on at once (SG).

steps.label: Heightened monitoring window
steps.detail: Watch the restarted system more closely than steady-state operation for a defined window afterward, so a recurrence is caught immediately rather than at the next scheduled review.
